questions.q: What is the main practical difference between a typical API key and a typical OAuth2 bearer token?
options: An API key is sent in the URL; a bearer token is sent in the response body
An API key is usually long-lived and assigned once; a bearer token is usually short-lived and issued by the API
There is no difference — they are two names for the same thing
A bearer token can only be used once and then must be deleted
questions.explain: An API key is typically a permanent secret assigned to an account, while a bearer token is typically short-lived and issued dynamically, often through a flow like OAuth2 client-credentials.

questions.q: In the OAuth2 client-credentials flow shown for PaymentPro, what two values does Northbridge's script trade for an access token?
options: A username and password
A client ID and client secret
An email address and API key
A session cookie and CSRF token
questions.explain: The client-credentials grant trades a client_id and client_secret, posted to the token endpoint, for a short-lived access token.

questions.q: Why does the example cache the access token's expiry with a 30-second buffer (expires_at = now + expires_in - 30) instead of using the exact expiry time?
options: To make the token last 30 seconds longer than the API allows
It has no real effect and is just a style choice
To refresh slightly before the real expiry, avoiding a request that starts right as the token dies mid-call
Because PaymentPro requires all requests to wait 30 seconds
questions.explain: The buffer ensures the code treats the token as expired a little early, so it refreshes proactively instead of risking a request failing because the token expired during the call.

questions.q: Where should PAYMENTPRO_CLIENT_ID and PAYMENTPRO_CLIENT_SECRET live in a script that calls this API?
options: Hardcoded as string literals directly in the Python file
In a comment above the function that uses them
In environment variables, read with os.environ, as covered in lesson 12
Embedded in the URL as query parameters
questions.explain: Credentials belong in environment variables rather than source code, so they never end up committed to version control or exposed in the codebase.

questions.q: What problem does caching the access token in get_access_token() solve?
options: It makes the JSON response smaller
It avoids requesting a brand-new token on every single API call, reusing a valid one until it's near expiry
It encrypts the token so PaymentPro can't read it
It automatically rotates the client secret
questions.explain: Without caching, every call to get_transactions() would re-request a token even when a valid one already exists, wasting requests and risking rate limits.
